lessonRef.title: Guided practice A: shape, outliers, and their effect on summaries

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Use this example as the model for the guided set below.

items.prompt: Ice cream sales correlate with drowning rates. Does ice cream cause drowning?

steps: A lurking variable explains the association.
workedSolution.answer: No; a third variable explains it

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: A data set records 9, 20, 2, 9, 12. Give the mean and the median.
choices: mean 9, median 10.4
mean 10, median 9
mean 10.4, median 9
mean 10.4, median 10

items.prompt: A data set of five values between 10 and 30 has one additional reading of 245 appended. Which statement best describes the effect on the mean and the median?
choices: The mean rises sharply while the median changes little, because the mean uses every value’s size.
The median rises sharply while the mean changes little.
Neither statistic changes, because one value cannot affect a summary.
Both the mean and the median rise sharply.

items.prompt: A two-way table has row 1: 5 yes, 17 no; row 2: 25 yes, 6 no. Among row-1 respondents, what fraction answered yes?
A least-squares line for a data set is ŷ = 5x + 42, where x is measured in hour studieds and y in test points. Interpret the slope.
choices: Each additional hour studied is associated with an increase of about 5 test points.
The predicted value is 5 test points when x is 0.
Each additional hour studied causes an increase of exactly 5 test points.
Each additional test points is associated with 5 more hour studieds.

items.prompt: Towns with more fire engines report more fire damage. What conclusion is justified?
choices: A third variable — warm weather — plausibly drives both, so correlation here is not evidence of causation.
Random assignment makes a causal conclusion reasonable, because the groups differ only by the treatment.
A strong correlation always establishes causation when the sample is large.
Larger towns have both more engines and more fires, so the association reflects town size rather than a causal link.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A data set records 12, 18, 14, 20, 16. Give the mean and the median.
choices: mean 16, median 16
mean 16, median 17
mean 16, median 14
mean 17, median 16

items.prompt: A data set of five values between 10 and 30 has one additional reading of 250 appended. Which statement best describes the effect on the mean and the median?
choices: The mean rises sharply while the median changes little, because the mean uses every value’s size.
Neither statistic changes, because one value cannot affect a summary.
The median rises sharply while the mean changes little.
Both the mean and the median rise sharply.

items.prompt: A two-way table has row 1: 9 yes, 36 no; row 2: 34 yes, 34 no. Among row-1 respondents, what fraction answered yes?

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Mastery check. Work without help, then stop and hand this section in.

items.prompt: A least-squares line for a data set is ŷ = 5x + 10, where x is measured in kilometre travelleds and y in litres of fuel. Interpret the slope.
choices: Each additional litres of fuel is associated with 5 more kilometre travelleds.
Each additional kilometre travelled is associated with an increase of about 5 litres of fuel.
Each additional kilometre travelled causes an increase of exactly 5 litres of fuel.
The predicted value is 5 litres of fuel when x is 0.

items.prompt: Ice cream sales and swimming-pool admissions are strongly positively correlated across a year. What conclusion is justified?
choices: A third variable — warm weather — plausibly drives both, so correlation here is not evidence of causation.
A strong correlation always establishes causation when the sample is large.
Random assignment makes a causal conclusion reasonable, because the groups differ only by the treatment.
Larger towns have both more engines and more fires, so the association reflects town size rather than a causal link.
